title: Local Genres Research for Scripture Translation

sections.label: Find & Describe Local Genres
sections.guidance: This is the starting point of the whole process: learn what genres your people have, before thinking about any one passage. Everything you record here is reusable for every passage you translate later.

children.label: 1a: Find Local Genres
children.guidance: A 'genre' is a kind of song, poem, story, or chant your people use. List the ones people enjoy, understand, and can still make and perform today. Catalog as many as make sense for your group — many teams find 5 to 20.

children.label: Your genre list

Need more genres? Use the prompts below to plan whom to ask, where to ask, and what to ask. Look for kinds of songs, poems, stories, and chants that people understand, enjoy, and can still create and perform today.
Who could we ask about genres? (for example: leaders, teachers, artists, mothers)
When and where could we ask? (for example: celebrations, festivals, holidays, gatherings, social media)
What questions can we ask? (for example: about births, weddings, funerals, and celebrations; and about how people use the voice, instruments, the body, and colors)

These prompts are only a few of many ideas for finding genres; see pages 67-69 of the CLAT Companion for more. For more on why local genres matter, see 'Why Consider Local Genres in Translation?' (Frost 2024).
1b: Genre Purpose
children.guidance: Three basic things about {genre}: a short description, the topics it usually covers, and the purposes it serves in the community. This is the information you will use later to match genres with passages.

children.label: Fill these in for the genre you are studying: {genre}. Who performs it, when, and what they use comes next, in 1c.
Describe {genre} briefly. What would you tell an outsider so they could recognize it?
children.example: A slow song sung by one voice with a bamboo flute, always at night, with long held notes at the end of each line.

children.label: What does the name of {genre} mean? Is there any word-play in the name?
What is {genre} usually about? What topics come up again and again?
children.example: A harvest song: about thanking the land for food, the work of planting, and the family eating together.

children.label: What is {genre} used to do in the community? Choose all that fit.
children.guidance: One genre can serve more than one purpose. For example, a genre could carry both laments and praise.

children.label: Say more about the purposes of {genre}. What function does it play? What does it help people do?
children.example: Sung at funerals to help the family cry together; also sung alone by widows. It helps people grieve as a group.

children.label: 1c: Social Features of {genre}
children.guidance: Picture a real performance of {genre}. Work through the who, when, where, and what questions, plus what the genre reminds people of and how loved it is. This is the information that helps a team choose wisely between genres later.

children.label: Who takes part in {genre}?
children.guidance: Note specific ages, genders, required status, or official roles of participants. Think of singers, players, leaders, dancers, and also the audience.
children.example: In a village hymn, a song leader starts each line and the whole gathering sings it back. Elders sit in front; children join the chorus.

children.label: When and where is {genre} performed? (the time, the place, the occasion)
children.example: At a wedding, in the evening, in the open yard. Or at a funeral, beside the house, the night before burial.

children.label: What materials/objects do people use in {genre}? (instruments, clothing, objects, props)
children.example: A large drum and a bamboo flute; the leader wears a special cloth; a carved staff is raised at the high point.

children.label: How are people placed in the space during {genre}? (who stands where, who faces whom, who moves)
children.example: The singers stand in a circle facing inward; the soloist steps into the middle for the most important verse.

children.label: What does {genre} remind people of? What associations do they have with it? (for example, a religious practice, a musical instrument, a type of dance, a certain topic, a particular kind of clothing, specific objects, politics, or customs)
children.example: It reminds people of old funeral chants, so using it for a joyful psalm could feel strange.

children.label: How popular and loved is {genre}? (Do people still use it and make new ones?)
children.help: Extinct: no one performs it anymore, and no one makes new pieces; it survives only in memory or recordings. Locked: a fixed set of old pieces is performed only for special occasions (festivals, cultural shows); no one performs it for everyday enjoyment, and no new pieces are made. Fading: fewer people perform it than before, and fewer new pieces are being made. Stable: people still perform it regularly, and new pieces keep being made at a steady rate. Thriving: more and more people perform it, and new pieces are being made all the time.

children.label: Is {genre} planned ahead, or made up on the spot?
children.guidance: Some genres are composed in advance and repeated; others are invented in the moment. Knowing which shows you where a translation has room to move.
children.example: The opening call is fixed and rehearsed; the middle verses are made up fresh each time.

children.label: Other notes on {genre}

sections.label: 1d: The Big Picture of {genre}

children.label: 1d.1: The Parts (Sections) of {genre}
How is {genre} ordered from start to finish? What usually comes first, next, and last?
What are the main parts of a full performance of {genre}? (How many parts, and what is each part for?)
children.footnote: Some genres flow straight through from start to finish and do not have clear separate parts.
children.example: A praise song might have an opening call, three verses, and a closing blessing — four parts.

children.label: How do the parts of {genre} relate to each other? (For example: repeated, opposite, or a changed version of another part.)
If {genre} has music, how do the parts fit the music? (For example: the same or a different tune for each line; a high point in the music that you can expect.)
Within a performance of {genre}, which person sings or speaks which lines or parts?

What tells the listener that one part of {genre} has ended and a new one has started? (For example: the topic, the mood, the rhythm or sound, who is speaking, the instruments, or the way the voice sounds.)
What usually marks the beginning, the middle, and the end of {genre}, both of the whole performance and of each part?
children.footnote: Examples: expected words, content, set phrases, performance features, pauses or timing, or a change in the space, the objects, or the people taking part. See the style pages (1e) for more ideas.

children.label: 1d.2: How {genre} Makes Things Stand Out (prominence)

How does {genre} make its most important idea(s) stand out? For example: by where it is placed; by repetition (a word, a line, a refrain, an antiphonal response); by a sudden change in volume or other voice feature; by a change in musical instrument; by packing many strong features together; by surprising the listener (explain how).
children.example: In a hymn, the whole group sings the refrain loudly together while one voice sings the verses, so the line everyone sings stands out. In a drumming song, the drum may suddenly stop, or beat harder, right at the key moment.

children.label: How does {genre} make the second-most important ideas stand out?
What tells the listener that the high point of {genre} has arrived?
children.footnote: This may overlap with the most important material above. If you have not done the detailed style study (1e) yet, make a note to come back and add to this answer later.

children.label: How does {genre} build up to its most beautiful or powerful moment, the part people will remember most?
children.footnote: Example: in Psalm 67, the middle verse is marked as special in several ways. This draws attention to the peoples of the world, and it sets up the main point of the psalm: that the ends of the earth will fear God.
children.example: A soloist sings alone and soft; then the drums enter and the whole group joins for the final, strongest verse. That build-up is the peak.

children.label: 1d.3: How {genre} Shows Feelings (Emotions)
What feelings usually appear in {genre}?
How does {genre} show each feeling? (Use one row per feeling.)
children.footnote: You can add to these answers using the detailed style features (1e). For example, a certain instrument may stand for sadness.

columns.label: Instruments, objects, or other things used

children.label: In {genre}, how much does understanding the feelings depend on the words themselves, and how much on other things like the tone of voice?
1d.4: How {genre} Links Related Ideas (connections)

There are four levels of "connected things". (1) Related WORDS: single words that go together, like "sing" and "song". (2) Related PHRASES: short groups of words said more than once, like "the LORD reigns". (3) Related PARTS: whole lines or sentences that match, like two lines built the same way (a part is a line or a sentence). (4) Related IDEAS: bigger thoughts that belong together even when the words are different, like "God saves" and "God protects". The chart below asks how {genre} shows each kind of connection.
How can {genre} help listeners see that ideas are connected?

columns.label: Position (for example, lines that are built the same way)
Things to look at (colors, flags, objects)
Word tricks (for example, words built from the same root, like 'sing / singer / song')

children.example: A hymn links two lines by giving them the same tune and the same number of beats (Position + Sounds). A praise chant links two ideas by repeating a hand-raise each time God's power is named (Body).

children.guidance: Good songs help listeners feel that things belong together. This page is about the ways {genre} shows that two things are connected, even when they are far apart in the song.

sections.guidance: Study one genre at a time. These four pages are about the big-picture shape of {genre}: its parts, how it makes things stand out, how it carries feelings, and how it ties ideas together.

sections.label: 1e: The Style & Details of {genre}
sections.guidance: The finer features of {genre}. On each page, record what you notice, then pull out the special features and mark each one Required or Common. The Required features drive the translation work later.

children.label: 1e.1: How {genre} Uses Words

Does this genre use set phrases or sayings? Where in the piece do they come? (For example, a saying like 'better to be poor and honest than rich and cruel.') Are some words repeated at the start of lines? Are names, or words like 'no' and 'not', used in special ways?
Does this genre play with words? (For example: words that sound alike, words with two meanings, jokes made with words, or two opposite ideas put side by side.)
What kind of language does this genre use? (For example: a special dialect or accent; polite, normal, or everyday speech; special or old words; borrowed words; rare words.)

Does this genre build its lines in special ways? (For example: saying the same thing twice in different words; a sentence that runs over into the next line; a question that does not need an answer; or leaving out a word that the listener already understands.)
Special word features of {genre} to remember
children.guidance: Pull out the 3 to 5 word features that stand out most from your answers above, and mark each one Required or Common.

columns.label: Part of the genre?
columns.help: Required means the genre is not itself without this feature — leaving it out breaks the genre. Common means it often appears, but a performance without it still counts as this genre. Example: in a lullaby, a soft, slow voice is Required; calling the child by name is Common — a lullaby without the name is still a lullaby.

children.label: 1e.2: How {genre} Is Put Together (Discourse)
Does the point of view change through the genre? (For example: is there a narrator? Does the speaker change? Does the person being spoken to change?)

How are people named or referenced in this genre? The first time someone is mentioned, how are they named? After that, do they use a short name, a word like 'he' or 'she', or no name at all? How does the listener know who is being talked about? (For example: first 'the old chief came'; after that, just 'he said'.)

How are action words (verbs) used? Do some carry the main story while others give background detail? Are some verb forms used only in certain parts (for example, one form for the main events and another for side comments)?
Describe the use of people's exact words (direct speech), and/or people's reported speech (indirect speech).
What, if any, small words (particles) appear again and again (for example, a word that means 'thus' or 'look!')?
Special discourse features of {genre} to remember
children.guidance: Pull out the 3 to 5 features that stand out most from your answers above, and mark each one Required or Common.

columns.label: Part of the genre?
columns.help: Required means the genre is not itself without this feature — leaving it out breaks the genre. Common means it often appears, but a performance without it still counts as this genre. Example: in a lullaby, a soft, slow voice is Required; calling the child by name is Common — a lullaby without the name is still a lullaby.

children.label: 1e.3: The Sounds of {genre}
How is the rhythm made? (For example: the number of beats or syllables in each line; a steady pulse you can feel; chanting.)
Does it use rhyme at the ends? (between words, between lines, or between verses?)
Are there other matching sounds? (For example: words that start with the same sound; the same vowel sound repeated; the same consonant sound repeated.) Where do they come, and how?
Does it use sounds that carry no meaning, like 'la-la-la' or 'hey'? Where do they appear, and what are they for?
Does it use words that imitate sounds or actions? (For example: 'boom' or 'splash', or a word that paints how something moves.)
If your language uses tones, how do the tones work together with the rhythm and the matching sounds above?
Special sound features of {genre} to remember
children.guidance: Pull out the 3 to 5 features that stand out most from your answers above, and mark each one Required or Common.

columns.label: Part of the genre?
columns.help: Required means the genre is not itself without this feature — leaving it out breaks the genre. Common means it often appears, but a performance without it still counts as this genre. Example: in a lullaby, a soft, slow voice is Required; calling the child by name is Common — a lullaby without the name is still a lullaby.

children.label: 1e.4: Picture-Language in {genre} (Figurative Language)
What picture-language does this genre use? Note whether it is used, and how (where in the piece, about what topics, alone or in groups).

options.label: A name for something closely linked to it (like 'the crown' for the king)
Personification (gives human traits to a thing)
Symbolism (a thing stands for an idea)
A gentle word for something hard to say
Stereotype (a fixed image of a group)
Idiom (a saying whose meaning is not its plain words)

children.label: What other ways does this genre use to paint pictures in the mind?
Special picture-language features of {genre} to remember
children.guidance: Pull out the 3 to 5 features that stand out most from your answers above, and mark each one Required or Common.

columns.label: Part of the genre?
columns.help: Required means the genre is not itself without this feature — leaving it out breaks the genre. Common means it often appears, but a performance without it still counts as this genre. Example: in a lullaby, a soft, slow voice is Required; calling the child by name is Common — a lullaby without the name is still a lullaby.

children.label: 1e.5: How {genre} Is Performed

How is the voice used? (For example: the rise and fall of the sound; fast or slow; clear or soft sounds; loud or quiet; the quality of the voice, such as rough, smooth, nasal, or breathy; how strong it is.) Say why it matters, what it does, how it changes through the piece, and the key places.
How does movement add to it? (body positions, gestures, facial expressions)
If your language uses tones, how do the tones work together with the voice features above?
Special performance features of {genre} to remember
children.guidance: Pull out the 3 to 5 features that stand out most from your answers above, and mark each one Required or Common.

columns.label: Part of the genre?
columns.help: Required means the genre is not itself without this feature — leaving it out breaks the genre. Common means it often appears, but a performance without it still counts as this genre. Example: in a lullaby, a soft, slow voice is Required; calling the child by name is Common — a lullaby without the name is still a lullaby.

children.label: 1e.6: Other Things You Notice in {genre}
Word order: is the order of the doer, the action, and the thing fixed? When does it change? Where in the line does a new idea (something the listener has not heard yet) usually appear?
How are parts joined together? (For example: repeating the last idea of one part at the start of the next, so the listener can follow.)
Are smaller forms placed inside this genre? (For example: a riddle or a proverb.) Which kind, and where?
What is repeated? (words, phrases, the shape of the text, themes, characters, or picture-language?)
How packed is it? (How much repetition? How much new information in each line? How fast do new ideas come?)
Anything else about this genre that does not fit the groups above?
Other special features of {genre} to remember
children.guidance: Pull out the features that stand out most from your answers above, and mark each one Required or Common.

children.label: 2a: Focus on {passage}
children.guidance: Name the passage you want to translate or turn into Scripture-art (for example, Psalm 13). Pick the passage to focus on below, or add a new one. This workspace works for any passage, not only psalms.

children.label: How will people use this translation / Scripture-inspired artistic creation? Will they sing it, listen to it, read it, or join in? Where will they use it? (Example: sung together in church.)
2b: Choose a Genre
children.guidance: First say what the passage is doing. Then compare its purpose with your genres' purposes, keep the top 3, look closely at the social factors, and choose one.

children.label: What is this passage doing?
children.guidance: Answer these from a trusted study process or resource. For example: the Psalms OBT Exegesis Worksheet (purpose is mostly in its section C), or 'Psalms: Layer by Layer' (see its overview sections and overview videos).

children.label: What is this passage mainly about? Write its specific message. (Example: it thanks God for healing from a sickness.)
What is the passage mainly doing? (For example: teaching, encouraging, or mourning.)
What kind of passage is it?

options.label: Lament (a sad cry to God for help)
Thanksgiving (thanks God for something he did)
Trust (says God can be relied on)

children.label: Genres that could work for this passage
children.footnote: Examples of problems: (1) Who takes part. The genre may be sung only by women, but the translation is meant for the whole church to sing together. (2) What it reminds people of. The genre may use a drum that is linked to worshiping ancestors or to calling on evil spirits.

columns.label: Any problems? (who uses it, when, or what it reminds people of)

children.label: Which genre will the team use for this passage?

children.label: 2e: Decisions & First Draft
You are ready to create. Keep prayer part of the work, and include people who enjoy making art in this genre. The summary below gathers the decisions you have made so far.
What you have decided so far
First draft and notes
Record your first draft (voice)
children.guidance: In oral contexts, speaking or singing a draft often works better than writing one. Record as many takes as you like; keep the ones worth keeping.

children.label: Two reminders. (1) Keep prayer part of the process, from start to finish. (2) This tool helps with the genre side of translation. You still need to check key words and sentence-level meaning carefully with your normal translation process.
